evidence_they_had_already_seen.note: 1 of 5 live theories are scored only on measurements that already existed when they were stated. That is not a fault by itself — a principle stated in round 6 has to explain rounds 1 to 5, and this is how it earns its way in. It is a different claim once a theory has met NO measurement made after it was written: nothing it said could have come out wrong. The measurement that would settle this for `Integrator-specific truncation constants` is one candidate it has not already seen: build a row that varies whatever it names and record it. If the theory holds there, it stops being a re-reading of what was already on the shelf.

no_outside_check.note: 6 candidates are ranked by `log10_max_jacobi_drift`, and not one of them came from outside this campaign. Every number in the record was produced by the same instrument, so the record cannot show that instrument to be wrong. The cheapest fix is one published value scored under `log10_max_jacobi_drift`, recorded with `origin: literature` and a `source_ref` — a single one is enough for a disagreement between your instrument and the world to become visible, and until there is one, a large gain in this record and a large error in this record are the same picture.

origin_audit.note: the best candidate was chosen by the campaign itself (6 of 6 labelled). This is the case where the machinery, rather than the reading, is what produced the result.

theories.statement: At these finite horizons RK4 error constants dominate; RK4 beats Yoshida despite not being symplectic.
Step size controls the dominant truncation error; halving h lowers drift before roundoff dominates.
Truncation dominates uniformly: smaller steps continue to lower Jacobi drift in both integrators.
Integrator-specific truncation constants compete with accumulating roundoff; repeated rotations can add a method-specific error floor at very small h.

what_to_do_next.note: the leading principle holds only 0.33 of the mass, so the evidence cannot yet separate the ones on the table. Widening the comparison is worth more than another round inside it: state a principle that would explain the same measurements a different way, or one naming a factor none of the current ones do.
